criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking/domestic (and farmstead livestock) water service access via collective rural water supply cooperatives outside municipal built-up zones in the Canton of Lucerne, Switzerland (despite the special-issue header mentioning irrigation communities, p. 4 explicitly clarifies that these schemes serve domestic uses and livestock production with almost no irrigation, and p. 5 and Note 4 confirm they provide regulated drinking-water infrastructure for households).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, administrative, regulatory, and governance arrangements shaping rural community water cooperatives, including New Public Management (WOV/NPM) administrative reforms and outsourcing. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyses concrete legal and administrative rules governing service access: (1) statutory spatial-planning demarcation (Raumplanungsgesetz) making municipalities responsible only inside urbanized zones while assigning legal self-responsibility to citizens outside built-up zones, structuring user-owned cooperative utility ownership; (2) statutory subsidy eligibility rules (targeting agricultural households) and cantonal administrative discretion in withholding federal subsidies from Cooperative N's independent reservoir refurbishment to compel scheme interconnection/merger; (3) regulatory enforcement ultimatums under national food-safety and drinking-water standards forcing reservoir upgrades; and (4) cooperative cost-recovery and organizational rules (flat-rate shared-reservoir cooperative vs. full merger and cross-subsidized pumping tariffs).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative socio-legal and actor-oriented institutional case study drawing on participant observation by the lead author during employment at the cantonal agency LAWA (Feb 2021–June 2022) and the private engineering consultancy (from July 2022), 17 in-depth semi-structured interviews (6 government officials, 5 scheme officials, 3 engineers, 2 local politicians, 1 contractor), and cantonal historical and newspaper archival research.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes relevant to community and household water service availability, reliability/continuity, infrastructure affordability/cost recovery, and scheme interconnection: drought-induced water rationing in Scheme K (11 households) lacking alternative sources; halted infrastructure renewal in Scheme S (14 households and 1 cheese factory) due to unaffordable reconstruction costs despite subsidies; inflated planning costs and reduced user consultation under NPM commercial engineering rates; forced abandonment of independent reservoir refurbishment by Cooperative N once federal subsidies were discretionarily withheld; household tariff concerns over cross-subsidizing pumping costs; and negotiated approval of a three-scheme interconnection under an umbrella reservoir cooperative preserving local low-cost voluntary O&M.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (rural households and collective water cooperatives outside built-up zones in Canton Lucerne, focusing on Schemes S [14 households + 1 cheese factory], K [11 households], and N, plus 17 interviewees), legal/administrative exposures, service-access and affordability/governance outcomes, and qualitative case-study design are clearly specified.

evidence_quotes.quote: Citizens outside of the built-up zone in the Canton of Lucerne, Switzerland are self-responsible to establish and maintain their water services. In response many independent, collective water schemes emerged in rural areas.
These schemes serve domestic uses and livestock production since only exceptional and very minor irrigated production takes place in the area.

These insights were enriched by in-depth, semi structured interviews with six government officials (four current and two former), five scheme officials, three engineers, two local politicians and one contractor. In addition, the historical and the newspaper archive of the Canton was consulted.

These reservoirs were constructed in 1970 and no longer met the minimum standard of the department of food security, that promptly issued an ultimatum forcing the cooperative to improve its infrastructure.
This project was stopped because the reconstruction cost was too high for the cooperative (despite subsidies) and the Canton received requests for subsidies from two neighbouring cooperatives.

the officials of the Canton decided that the independent refurbishment of the reservoirs of scheme N would not be allocated any federal subsidies. Without these subsidies, it would become too expensive for cooperative N to pursue the independent refurbishment of their own reservoirs and they would instead be forced to join the inter-connection option.

raw_response.exposure: Statutory spatial-planning self-responsibility outside urbanized zones (cooperative utility ownership), federal/cantonal agricultural drinking-water subsidy eligibility rules and cantonal administrative discretion in withholding subsidies, drinking-water/food-safety regulatory enforcement ultimatums, and New Public Management (WOV/NPM) outsourcing of technical planning to commercial engineering consultants
raw_response.outcome: Household and community drinking-water service establishment, drought reliability/water rationing, infrastructure refurbishment and planning affordability, tariff/pumping cost-sharing arrangements, and multi-scheme interconnection vs. cooperative autonomy
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural farming and non-farming households and user-owned collective water supply cooperatives outside built-up zones in the Canton of Lucerne, Switzerland; focal case study of three cooperatives (Scheme S serving 14 households and 1 cheese factory; Scheme K serving 11 households; and Scheme N) plus 17 semi-structured interview respondents (6 government officials, 5 scheme officials, 3 engineers, 2 local politicians, 1 contractor) and participant observation (2021–2022)
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6). Although published under a special-issue banner referencing irrigation communities, the text explicitly establishes that the studied Swiss rural cooperatives provide regulated household drinking/domestic water and livestock water (with negligible irrigation) outside municipal built-up zones. It examines concrete rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2—including statutory spatial-planning boundaries assigning rural water provision to citizen self-responsibility/cooperatives, drinking-water quality enforcement ultimatums, NPM statutory outsourcing rules, and cantonal administrative discretion in withholding federal infrastructure subsidies—and documents qualitative empirical outcomes for infrastructure affordability, drought supply reliability, cost-sharing rules, and interconnection of rural household water schemes. Per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal studies are included for mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking a quantitative effect estimate.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative ethnographic and actor-oriented institutional case study (participant observation, 17 semi-structured interviews, and archival research)
